newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-DOWN AT THE OLD DOG AND DUCK-BY TONY TWINE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-DOWN AT THE OLD DOG AND DUCK-BY TONY TWINE.

text.p: By Tony Twine, an economist at Econometrix financial consultancy

Once upon a time, there was a drake called Bill and a dog called Bob. Bill had been given his name because his parents had recognised his prominent beak would become useful in talking his way both into and out of Situations. Bob was a doleful looking bloodhound, who had enlisted as a war dog -- his tail had been cut short on the day that he enlisted, and he had been known as Bob ever since.

Bill and Bob worked together at a public house in their nation's capital, appropriately named the Dog and Duck. Despite his military background, Bob had chosen to serve the public -- those not particularly well disposed towards him hinted that he enjoyed the tips. Others said that Bill not only enjoyed the tips, but the whole thing. After trying his hand at property development, Bill, through his enthusiasm and with lots of help from his health conscious wife, quickly rose to the head waiter of the establishment.

About four years after he had become head waiter, the owners of the Dog and Duck decided to undertake a routine and a regular check of public opinion regarding the head waiter and his circle of senior waiters. Not all of the waiters and other staff at the Dog and Duck thought that Bill should be the head waiter, but there was a genuine shortage of talent with which to replace him. Much to everybody's surprise, Bob suddenly resigned his job as a senior waiter, and entered the campaign to displace Bill.

Part of Bob's campaign was an attempt to convince the staff and clients of the Dog and Duck that he could shorten the queues of the unemployed. Bill countered by saying that he too was trying to keep everybody off the dole, in more than one sense of the word. In fact, the similarity of the claims of the two contestants soon came to be the dominant feature of their campaigns to become head waiter.

The truth of the matter was that, because of the vast size and complexity of the operations of the Dog and Duck, there was precious little that could be done differently either in promise or practice by either of the two campaigners. A little twist here, or a tweak there, and that was about all that could be offered by way of differentiation to the supporters, workers and management of the public house.

Both Bob and Bill realised the importance of packaging their scarcely differentiated intentions -- the packaging frequently providing the only differentiation, although the mass of the general public were not always aware that this was the case. Each candidate's supporters thought, for instance, that there was a vital difference between a menu which had hotdogs at the top, with duck a l'orange further down, or vice versa. The fact that, irrespective of their order of listing, both appeared on the menu, seemed to escape not only the keen supporters of Bill and Bob respectively, but the paying public at large.

So, on the anniversary of the plot by the only politician in history who had been apprehended taking a barrel or two into the cellars of a public house, the customers of the Dog and Duck went along to choose the next head waiter of that fine establishment. At the end of the process, a portulant lady who had clearly frequently indulged herself on many occasions on that emporium's fine cuisine, was heard to break out into song.

When the result was made public, Bob sucked in his breath, but Bill continued to refuse to inhale. Life went on pretty much the way it had done before the race to be appointed had begun, for everybody except the close circle of friends of the loser. Once the dust had settled, the customers came to realise that their pocketbooks were no worse off than they had been when Bill and Bob were battling for the top position. They still paid the same prices for the same items on the menu -- many paid whether they ate or drank at the Dog and Duck or not. Others, simple tradesmen like you and I, sold to and bought from the establishment, and wondered what life would have been like under the head waitership of the third (and largely unnoticed) candidate for the job, whose name sounded a little like a French aniseed liquor, poured over ice from an antarctic ice shelf. Then again, perhaps that might have led to too much foreign influence, heaven help the Dog and Duck if it lead to any form of free trade. Having a slimmed down lady singing at the end, would, after all, simply not be the same.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
